results.title: FLOP and FLOPs – SolveForce Unified Intelligence
results.content: # FLOP and FLOPs. 1. **FLOP**: This stands for **Floating Point Operation**. It denotes a single floating point operation. 2. **FLOPs**: This stands for **Floating Point Operations Per Second**. It’s a measure of computing speed and represents how many floating-point calculations a CPU, GPU, or another computing device can perform in one second. The “s” in FLOPs emphasizes the operations per second. When discussing the computing performance or benchmarking results, “FLOPs” (with the ‘s’) is more commonly used since it represents a rate of performance over time. For example, “This GPU can perform 2 teraFLOPs” means the GPU can perform 2 trillion floating point operations per second. In the context of computers, especially when discussing high-performance computing, FLOPs are a common benchmark to gauge computational power. Here are some key points about FLOPs:. **Scale**: FLOPs can be measured on various scales, including:. * KiloFLOP (KFLOP) – Thousands of FLOPs. * MegaFLOP (MFLOP) – Millions of FLOPs. * GigaFLOP (GFLOP) – Billions of FLOPs. * TeraFLOP (TFLOP) – Trillions of FLOPs. * PetaFLOP (PFLOP) – Quadrillions of FLOPs. * ExaFLOP (EFLOP) – Quintillions of FLOPs. **Usage**: FLOPs are typically used to measure the performance of supercomputers and high-end graphics cards, especially in tasks like scientific simulations, data analysis, and graphical rendering. **Not the Only Metric**: While FLOPs measure raw computational power, they’re not the only metric to consider. Other factors, like memory bandwidth, latency, and storage speed, can also impact the overall performance of a computer system. **Real-World Performance**: Just because a computer or GPU has a high FLOP rating doesn’t mean it will always perform at that level for every task. The real-world performance can vary based on software optimization, the specific nature of the tasks, and other hardware constraints. **Relation to Gaming and Graphics**: In the world of gaming and graphics rendering, FLOPs are often used to measure the computational power of GPUs. A higher FLOP value usually indicates a more powerful GPU, capable of rendering more complex graphics or handling advanced computational tasks. In summary, FLOP is a key metric in the world of computing, especially for high-performance systems, to give a quantitative measure of the system’s ability to handle floating-point calculations.

results.title: How does batching work on modern GPUs? - by Finbarr Timbers
results.content: The batched calculation requires Nx the compute to run, and, in fact, if you run this on CPU, you’ll see that this is true (average inference time for ResNet50, Colab):. Going from a batch size of 1, to 2, to 3 requires no additional time, and then after that it increases linearly. We can approximate the time it takes to transfer the weights by calculating the model size / memory bandwidth ratio, and approximate the time it takes to do the calculation by model FLOPS / GPU FLOPS. With an MLP, the FLOPS are approximately 2 \* the number of parameters \* the number of elements in the batch (2 \* m \* n \* b for a batch size of *b* and a *m x n* matrix). \(\frac{1}{\text{memory bandwidth}} = \frac{2 \cdot B}{\text{GPU FLOPS}}\). \(\frac{\text{GPU FLOPS}}{2\cdot\text{memory bandwidth}} = B\). When the batch size is less than the ratio of FLOPS to memory bandwidth, we are bottlenecked by memory bandwidth. There’s some noise, but it’s basically what we’d expect: inference time starts increasing dramatically around the ~128 mark (here, we double the batch size, so we see batches at 128, 256, and then 512). What’s also interesting is that the smaller networks don’t really see any scaling, taking roughly constant time across the entire range of batch sizes (from 1 to 512). In reinforcement learning (RL) research, particularly for researchers who work on continual learning problems, where there’s a single agent taking a long stream of actions, it’s often not worth it to use a GPU for experiments unless either 1) you have a very large network or 2) you extensively optimize every other aspect of your stack (if you want to make an old DeepMind engineer squirm, ask them about in-graph environments— at one point, we were implementing RL environments within the tensorflow graph). In a convolutional network, the weights are equal to the number of filters times the filter size. This means that, basically, for a convolutional layer, there’s much less advantage to batching, as we’re reusing the same weights many, many times.

results.title: Microbenchmarks - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Microbenchmarks are custom tests designed to evaluate specific components of a GPU, such as the instruction pipeline or global memory, by measuring their performance metrics like throughput. Microbenchmarks are designed to serve as specific stressors that sensitize targeted processor chips to particular failure modes under harsh environments, enabling the identification or diagnosis of deficiencies in traditional architecture performance metrics such as instructions per cycle and cache misses, as well as power or energy-related metrics, temperature and lifetime reliability, and resilience under transient errors. In the context of graphics processing unit (GPU) kernel performance, custom microbenchmarks are constructed to exercise different components of the target GPU, such as the instruction pipeline or global memory, and measure their throughput. Microbenchmarks are also applied to evaluate central processing unit (CPU) instruction throughput, memory latency and bandwidth, and cache behavior, as well as to construct power models for individual sub-units by correlating performance monitoring counters with empirical power measurements. Within Internet of Things (IoT) deployments, microbenchmarks provide useful information for understanding the performance of subsystems associated with smart objects, identifying architectural bottlenecks, and enabling hardware and software engineers to compare and assess design trade-offs at the component level. In GPU performance modeling, custom microbenchmarks are used to measure throughput and exercise different components such as instruction pipelines and global memory. In large-scale Internet of Things deployments, microbenchmarks provide useful information to understand subsystem performance, identify architectural bottlenecks, and allow engineers to compare and assess design trade-offs at the component level. The design of microbenchmarks requires flexibility and generality, allowing users to control code generation at the assembly level and specify both high-level and dynamic properties, such as loads per instruction and instructions per cycle ratio. The “architecture back-end” consists of three components: (a) definition of the instruction set architecture via op code syntax table, as well as the high-level parametric definition of the processor microarchitecture; (b) an analytical reference model that is able to calculate (precisely or within specified bounds) the performance and unit-level utilization levels of a candidate loop microbenchmark; (c) a (micro)architecture translator segment that is responsible for final (micro)architecture-specific consolidation and integration of the microbenchmark program.

results.title: GPU-STREAM: Benchmarking the achievable memory ...
results.content: GPU-STREAM: Benchmarking the achievable memory bandwidth of Graphics Processing Units Tom Deakin∗and Simon McIntosh-Smith† Department of Computer Science University of Bristol Bristol, UK Email: ∗tom.deakin@bristol.ac.uk, †simonm@cs.bris.ac.uk Abstract—Many scientiﬁc codes consist of memory bandwidth bound kernels — the dominating factor of the runtime is the speed at which data can be loaded from memory into the Arithmetic Logic Units. I. MEASURING MEMORY BANDWIDTH The STREAM Benchmark [1] measures the time taken for each of four simple kernels to be run (α is a scalar constant): 1) Copy: c[i] = a[i] 2) Multiply: b[i] = αc[i] 3) Add: c[i] = a[i] + b[i] 4) Triad: a[i] = b[i] + αc[i] It is simple to calculate how many bytes each of these kernels requires to be read from and written to memory, assuming perfect caching.

results.title: #29 Memory Bandwidth Engineering: The True Bottleneck in LLM GPU Architecture
results.content: # #29 Memory Bandwidth Engineering: The True Bottleneck in LLM GPU Architecture. GPU architecture limitations often create bottlenecks in large language model systems. Yet many teams struggle to achieve optimal performance while deploying LLMs. Large-batch inference in LLMs stays memory-bound, and DRAM bandwidth saturation emerges as the biggest problem. The GPU architecture's optimization doesn't always match LLM workloads, which creates unexpected performance limits. > "Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) are essential for training and running LLMs due to their ability to handle parallel computations." — Label Your Data Team, AI data labeling and model training experts. GPU architecture represents specialized hardware designed to perform massive parallel computations through thousands of small processing units working in sync. * Tensor cores: Specialized units built for matrix multiplication operations in LLM workloads. Modern GPU tensor cores speed up matrix operations in LLM workloads dramatically. LLM operation loads model weights from DRAM into SMs for computation. System performance depends more on moving billions of parameters between memory and compute units efficiently than raw computational power . GPUs handle LLM workloads differently from CPUs. The GPU architecture follows specific execution patterns that allow massive parallel processing but trades off some flexibility. NVIDIA GPUs run LLM operations through a system called thread blocks. These versatile processors handle sequential processing, support high-precision operations (FP32/FP64), and manage various GPU computing tasks . The delicate balance between memory bandwidth and computational power determines how LLM systems perform. This fundamental metric shows the ratio of computational operations (FLOPs) to memory bytes accessed during execution . Your system becomes memory-bound when the workload's arithmetic intensity falls lower than your GPU's OPs:Byte ratio. ### GPU memory architecture and HBM saturation. HBM acts as the main storage for model weights and intermediate values in GPU memory architecture. A Batching Configuration Advisor (BCA) helps optimize memory allocation and frees up GPU memory resources without fully hurting throughput . * GPU Memory Usage: The VRAM needed for model weights and activations. This usually points to memory bandwidth limits rather than compute power issues—a common challenge in LLM inference. DRAM bandwidth limits, not raw computational power, hold back LLM performance in most cases.
